utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated. Registrar, could you call the case, please, before the parties identify themselves? What is the number of the case?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is IT-95-13-D, the Prosecutor versus Mile Mrksic, Veselin Sljivancanin, and Miroslav Radic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Could we have the appearances for the party, not for both parties, only one, but the Office of the Prosecutor who has asked that this hearing be held and has filed the formal request.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If Your Honours please, my name is Niemann, and I appear with my colleague, Mr. Waespi, on behalf of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. We are going to ask you to explain why you have filed this request, but before doing so, I would like to turn to the registrar. I know that this is a proposal for deferral by a State, that is, in this case, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, but I believe that this State had been invited, as is indicated in our text, had been invited to appear. Can you report on this issue to the Trial Chamber, please, Mr. Registrar? Would you explain why the Defence, if we can call it that, is not here? Could you explain that?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, on the 7th of December, we announced that a hearing would take place before Trial Chamber I in respect of a request for deferral and pursuant to Rule 74 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. We also announced this to the State. In this case, we sent our correspondence to the Ambassador of Yugoslavia, indicating that he could appear as an amicus curiae at this hearing. We then received an answer, that is, we received it this morning, from the Embassy of Yugoslavia, according to which -- to indicate that he would not be here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Were you given any explanations?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: No. The letter was short and the letter was simply given to us and simply said that a representative was not in the position to be present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Did you say that he was not in that position or that he didn't want to?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The translation says that he is not in a position to. That's the translation we have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. That he is not in a position to be here. Did he express a desire that the hearing be postponed or give any other reasons?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: No, he did not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Could we ask the interpreters to translate the letter for us, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I can read it to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Do you read Serbo-Croat, Mr. Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: No, the translation we received. It is from a letter that was originally written in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. We move from Serbo-Croat into English and now into translations. All right. Read it to us, please, and that way we can translate it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We didn't get anything in Serbo-Croat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. All right. Read the letter, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: "Further to your letter of 7 December, 1998, I regret to inform you that a representative of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia will not be in a position to appear as an amicus curiae before Trial Chamber I of the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia. The Federal Republic of Yugoslavia reiterates fully their request for legal assistance which was expressed in a letter from the Military Tribunal of Belgrade. The Federal Republic of Yugoslavia also requests the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia to agree to the Belgrade Military Tribunal's request. Yours truly," and it is signed by the Ambassador, Milan Gorbic, and it's a letter that was sent to the Deputy Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you very much. I think that my colleagues will agree with me when I interpret it and say that it is simply not a question of a physical or geographic problem which might have had us postpone this hearing, rather, it is a position of principle on the part of the Embassy of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia which says that the real question has to be dealt with, this request for assistance in respect of a trial which is being initiated on its territory with Miroslav Radic and, therefore, they did not consider it suitable or timely to come to appear at this hearing. Having indicated those conditions, I will speak with my colleagues very quickly to see what their opinion is. The Judges consider that this is a very clearly expressed option by the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and under those conditions, the Republic, in its answer, maintains its own request for assistance, and the Judges consider that they can now deal with the request from the Prosecutor asking the Republic of Yugoslavia to defer its case on the basis of certain factual and legal reasons that will be given to us now by the Prosecutor. Mr. Prosecutor, the floor is yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If Your Honours please, and as detailed and set out in our proposal, this is a proposal under Article 9(2) of the Statute of the Tribunal and in accordance with the Rules, in particular Rule 9, paragraphs 2 and 3 of the Rules of the Tribunal. Your Honours, it relates to an investigation concerning certain events that occurred at the Vukovar hospital in November of 1991 when some 260 unarmed men were massacred at a grave site near the city of Vukovar, arising out of which an indictment was prepared in relation to, in particular, three individuals, Mile Mrksic, Veselin Sljivancanin, and Miroslav Radic. This has been an ongoing matter for some time, if Your Honours please, in the Tribunal. There was, in connection with this, a hearing under Rule 61 of the Rules and various requests have been made to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in connection with requesting the surrender of these three individuals against whom arrest warrants have been issued. The proposal by the Prosecutor in this case is different from other proposals made in previous cases. In previous cases, the Prosecutor has sought deferral under Rule 9, paragraph 3, which relates to a matter which has significant factual and legal questions associated with an investigation or prosecution. In this case, the application is made also under paragraph 2 of Rule 9, and that part of paragraph 2 which relates to proceedings are designed to shield the accused from international criminal responsibility. It's the contention of the Prosecutor that this is more germane to this application or proposal than what has ever been the case in previous proposals under Rule 9 for a deferral. If Your Honours please, the details are set out in greater particularity in our application, and I don't wish to trouble Your Honours by rehearsing those details which are there and available for Your Honours to examine, save this, that notwithstanding considerable attempts, a number of attempts to secure the arrest of these three accused persons, such attempts have not been successful, and now the point has been reached where a proceeding has been commenced in a Military Court in Belgrade, the outcome of which we can't be certain of but we assume will then proceed to deal with the subject matter of the indictment that has been filed by the Prosecutor in this Tribunal. The Prosecutor has no faith in the outcome of those proceedings having regard to the history of this matter. Your Honours, it may be perhaps best for me to present to you a history, a concise history of the events that lead us to this point. If I am permitted to recite from correspondence that has passed from the President of this Tribunal to the Security Council and then to recite to you the resolution of the Security Council and then to conclude with an address given by the President of the Tribunal to the Security Council as recently as yesterday on these matters, and if I may be permitted, in summary form, to go through those three matters, I think it would best present the background upon which we seek to rely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Prosecutor. The Tribunal, since this is a public hearing, would like the entire procedure, which is very long, very expensive, costs a lot of money, costs a lot of man hours, and which shows the position that each party has taken in respect of the -- yes, you may continue, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If Your Honours please, the President of the Tribunal -- both Presidents, in fact, President Cassese and President McDonald, have both written to the Security Council in the past concerning this matter. President McDonald has, in fact, written three letters to the Security Council that I'm aware of, but I only seek to go to one, and I will summarise it as best I can, but I think referring to the text of her letter is helpful in understanding this matter. On the 8th of September, 1998, she wrote in the following terms to the President of the Security Council. "Excellency, I have the honour to report to the Security Council the continuing refusal of the Government of the Republic of Yugoslavia (Serbia and Montenegro) (F.R.Y.) to cooperate with the International Tribunal by failing to arrest and transfer to the custody of the International Tribunal three persons indicted by the International Tribunal: Mile Mrksic, Miroslav Radic, and Veselin Sljivancanin. I am bringing this to the attention of the Security Council at the request of the Presiding Judge of Trial Chamber I and in the context of recent initiatives by the United Nations to uphold and develop international criminal law. "The International Tribunal indicted the three individuals on 7 November 1995, for the murder of 260 unarmed men following the fall of the city of Vukovar in November 1991. A warrant for their arrest was issued and transmitted to, inter alia, the Government of the F.R.Y., as the accused were believed to be residing on its territory. As that warrant was not executed, the Judge who confirmed the Indictment ordered the Prosecutor to submit the case for a review by a panel of three Judges. On 3 April 1996, Trial Chamber I concluded that there exists sufficient grounds for believing that Mile Mrksic, Miroslav Radic, and Veselin Sljivancanin committed the offences with which they were charged in the Indictment and certified that the failure to effect service of the Indictment was due to the refusal of the F.R.Y. to cooperate with the Tribunal. The Trial Chamber further issued international arrest warrants against the three accused which were subsequently transmitted to all States and to the Implementation Force established under Annex 1-A of the General Framework Agreement for Peace in Bosnia and Herzegovina," otherwise known, Your Honours, as the Dayton Agreement. "Acting upon the recommendation of the Trial Chamber, my predecessor, President Cassese, on 24 April 1996 reported the refusal of the F.R.Y. to arrest the three men. President Cassese noted that in not only refusing to comply with the orders of the International Tribunal but in promoting, supporting, and continuing to pay one of the indicted men, the F.R.Y. demonstrated its disregard and disrespect for the obligations under international law. On 8 May 1996, the President of the Security Council reminded the F.R.Y. of those obligations, 'deplor[ed the] failure ... to execute the arrest warrants' and called for the immediate execution of the warrants. He further stated that the Security Council would remain seized of the matter. "Since that date, the three individuals have remained at liberty, alleged to be residing in Serbia. Indeed, the authorities of the F.R.Y. have not refuted such allegations. The Office of the Prosecutor of the International Tribunal has repeatedly demanded the arrest of the accused. On 19 December 1997, following a request from the Prosecutor, Trial Chamber II ordered the authorities to serve the accused with the Indictment and various other documents and to notify the Registrar of the whereabouts of the accused. On the same day, Trial Chamber II requested the authorities to ensure the publication in the F.R.Y. of a notice to the accused to surrender immediately to the International Tribunal." Madam President then goes on. "The persistent and continuing rejection of orders to arrest Mile Mrksic, Miroslav Radic, and Veselin Sljivancanin is but the most blatant example of the refusal of the F.R.Y. to cooperate with the International Tribunal. Such intransigence has formed a consistent pattern since the International Tribunal was established by the Security Council in resolution 827 of 27 May 1993. Notable in this regard is failure to take necessary measures under domestic law to implement provisions of resolution 827 and the Statute of the International Tribunal, as required by paragraph 4 of the resolution. Indeed, the F.R.Y. remains the only signatory to the Dayton Agreement that has neither adopted legislation to facilitate cooperation with the International Tribunal, nor taken steps to transfer to the International Tribunal's custody those three indictees on its territory. "Put simply, such conduct is illegal. The Security Council acted under Chapter Seven of the United Nations Charter when it created the International Tribunal. In his report to the Security Council prior to the adoption of resolution 827, the Secretary General noted that Orders of the International Tribunal have the status of actions under Chapter 7. Thus, all States are legally required to comply with its orders, including warrants of arrest and surrender. Moreover, the F.R.Y., as a signatory to the Dayton Agreement, is further bound to cooperate with the International Tribunal." And then Her Honour goes on to refer to other matters in this letter which she seeks to place before the Security Council. Following that, Your Honours, on the 17th of November, 1998, the Security Council passed resolution 1207. In resolution 1207, the Security Council calls upon the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and all other States which have not already done so to take measures necessary under domestic law to implement the provisions of resolution 827 and affirms that a State may not invoke provisions of domestic law as justification for its failure to perform binding obligations under international law. The Security Council then go on to condemn the failure to date of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia to execute the arrest warrants issued by the Tribunal against the three individuals referred to by President McDonald in her letter of the 8th of September, 1998 that I have just read out to Your Honours. The Security Council then goes on to demand the immediate unconditional execution of those arrest warrants, including the transfer to the custody of the Tribunal of those individuals. Your Honours, following the passage of resolution 1207, the Security Council subsequently invited President McDonald to inform them of the progress that had been made in terms of cooperation with the Tribunal between the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and the Tribunal since the passage of that resolution. As recently as yesterday, President McDonald presented her response to the Security Council on the progress that had been made in terms of cooperation with the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. In her response, she not only deals with this issue but she also deals with matters pertaining to events in Kosovo. I will skip over the matters about Kosovo and go directly to what she says about her view of cooperation with the Tribunal as a consequence of the passage of resolution 1207 by the Security Council. She says as follows. "The Federal Republic of Yugoslavia is also in non-compliance with its obligations under international law, the U.N. Charter, Security Council resolution 827 establishing the Tribunal, and most recently, Security Council resolution 1207, by failing to execute arrest warrants on the three individuals referred to in my letter of 8 September 1998 to the President of the Security Council. Now, however, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia has not only failed to execute the arrest warrants, it has boldly refused to do so. "In a letter of 18 November 1998 to the Tribunal, the President of the Military Court in Belgrade advised that it intended to conduct certain 'investigative proceedings ... in connection with the criminal offence of war crimes against prisoners of war ... committed in the Vukovar hospital in November 1991 after a large number of members of the paramilitary formations of the Republic of Croatia were taken prisoner.' Further, it was stated in the letter that 'since in the course of the investigation this Court is also going to hear the testimonies of' [the three individuals named in the arrest warrants of the Tribunal], it wished a copy of the criminal case file and evidence which formed the basis of the indictment issued against these individuals by the Prosecutor of the Tribunal. It was requested that all available evidence be forwarded by 17 December 1998, because these individuals are scheduled to testify on that day." President McDonald then goes on. "Thus, not only is the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia failing to abide by the explicit requirements of Security Council resolution 1207, it is taking action in direct contravention of that resolution. "On 3 December 1998," she then goes on to say that the Prosecutor filed this proposal that now comes before Your Honours to deal with, and she sets out the law which she says founds the establishment of the Tribunal and the fact that it has primacy over courts in the former Yugoslavia. Your Honours, I went to the trouble of taking up Your Honours' time to read you that because I wished to alert you of the level that this matter has now reached since those early days when first the indictment and arrest warrant was issued, which was then subsequently followed by the public Rule 61 hearing, which was then followed by international arrest warrants and by requests to the Security Council, and to give Your Honours the background of the amount of effort that has been put in to try and persuade the Republic of Yugoslavia to cooperate with the Tribunal in accordance with its obligations under international law. There can be absolutely no doubt of the fact that it is fully aware of its obligations, and there can be absolutely no doubt of the fact that it has full information of the Prosecution that is sought to be brought by the Office of the Prosecutor. It is our respectful submission, Your Honours, that by putting this matter before a Military Court in Belgrade is no more than one further attempt on behalf of that State to circumvent the operations of this Tribunal and to frustrate the requirements of international law in bringing these persons to justice in The Hague. If Your Honours please, the purpose of this application is to remind, in this case, the Military Court itself of the obligations that are borne by the Republic of Yugoslavia, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, to comply with its international obligations and to surrender these three individuals to the competence of this Court. As set out by President McDonald, there is no question that this Tribunal has primacy over the courts of that State. There is no question that this is an investigation that was initiated well before any issue of investigating the matter was considered in Belgrade, in Serbia, or any other part of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. It is our respectful submission, Your Honours, that the basis upon which we seek this -- or we propose this request is clearly made out having regard to the history of the matter, that there is no question that these proceedings will be or are designed to shield the accused from international criminal responsibility and can be seen as no other basis. Unless I can assist Your Honours, those are my submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Niemann. The question which is being asked today in public is a crucial one, crucial for international justice, for which our mission is to ensure it is carried out, and it is a decision of the entire International Community as expressed in the resolution of May 1993. This is a very serious matter. We have reached the end of the proceedings, or the process, rather, and I think that if the Trial Chamber is intervening, it is because it is the Trial Chamber which confirmed the indictment, and the same Trial Chamber held a Rule 61 hearing which is provided for in case there is failure to execute a warrant of arrest, but I want these proceedings to be very well limited not only for the public in the court today but for all the appropriate authorities who follow our work. Let me remind you, this is not a new request for a warrant of arrest; that is not in this proposal. The issue is more complicated than that. It is a question of applying two provisions of our Statute and the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, one that provides that domestic courts can be competent to try criminal offences, that is genocide, crimes against humanity, violations of the Geneva Conventions and violations of the laws and customs of war, which is in our very founding Statute, and in them we read that national courts can try those cases. But the Statute also provides that there is always primacy for the International Tribunal in order to assert that the trial of those crimes exceeds at certain times what can be done on the level of domestic courts. The discussion is limited through application of our Rules of Procedure and Evidence which give further details on the conditions under which the International Tribunal can ask for deferral from a national court for all procedures that may have been initiated before those courts. Let me remind you that if the Prosecutor considers that in any such investigation or criminal proceedings instituted in the courts of any State, that is, the ones that have been initiated in Belgrade today before a Military Court, if it appears to the Prosecutor that proceedings are characterised as an ordinary crime, then we have nothing further to say. But if it shows that the procedure would not be impartial or independent or that the investigations or proceedings are designed to shield the accused from international criminal responsibility or the case is not diligently prosecuted, that's the very heart of what we are talking about here; or (3), if what is in issue is closely related to or otherwise involves significant factual or legal questions which may have implications for investigations or prosecutions before the Tribunal, the Prosecutor may propose to the Trial Chamber, designated by the President, that a formal request be made that such court defer to the competence of the Tribunal. These are the terms of the issue that we have to resolve. Therefore, I consider there is no ambiguity. We are not here to issue arrest warrants which don't have to be issued because three of the people involved have already been named in warrants of arrests and have been given to the International Community, and therefore, the International Community has the obligation to arrest those people, specifically the country in which they are residing today. So let things be clear, Mr. Niemann. The question that I wanted to ask you is not merely a formal one. The Judges are here in order to apply the Rules as impartially as possible, but I am going to go back to that word "impartial." Can you give specific reasons why you feel that there may be a lack of impartiality and that there would be a kind of political burden on the part of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, that is Serbia and Montenegro, which would now want to initiate proceedings before a Military Tribunal? I think that's the issue. That through its organs, the Tribunal has never denied the fact that domestic courts may try crimes that may have been committed in its territory, but insofar as we have to respond to your proposal, we would like to be informed of your point of view on this question of lack of impartiality. I see there is a coincidence here. Can you give us the reasons that you are stating that, because we are not here, as I have already said, in order to issue a new warrant of arrest. Mr. Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We are not seeking from Your Honours an arrest warrant. I just confirm that. If we do wish to pursue the course of arrest warrant, we would do that before the duty judge as we would ordinarily do, but that is not the question. But to respond directly to what Your Honour has raised, our position is this: We say that the proceedings before the Belgrade Military Court are designed to shield the accused from international criminal responsibility, and why we say that is this: The arrest warrant, the indictment and arrest warrant in this case, have been long outstanding, since 7 November, 1995. Since that time, no action has been taken against those three accused in any way, shape, or form, to punish them as a consequence of the crimes that we allege were committed at Vukovar in November of 1991. Every attempt that we have made to bring them to justice -- and I have recited just a few of those attempts that have been made -- have been resisted or otherwise ignored by the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. This situation probably would and probably may continue indefinitely except the reason why we say that the proceedings at this particular point in time are significant is that a number of issues have been brought to the attention of the Security Council very recently in relation to the behaviour of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, especially in connection with the events that have occurred most recently in Kosovo. Not only are the events in Kosovo an issue which has been dealt with by the Security Council and raised by the President of this Tribunal, but in conjunction with those matters, the continued failure by that State to comply with its international obligations has also been raised in conjunction with those matters. The point I make is this, Your Honours: That because of the increasing pressure that is being placed on the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia as a consequence of its failure to comply with its international obligations would, we suggest, lead them to the conclusion that one way to attempt to resolve one issue that confronts them -- putting aside Kosovo -- would be to try these people and say, "There. We've dealt with it, so you need no longer be concerned with the matter." We concern ourselves with that because we don't believe that that would be a genuine exercise of justice, it would merely be a sham in order to put off the International Community, in order to reduce the pressure that is being placed upon them because of their failure to comply with their international obligations. There is no coincidence, in our submission, between the fact that the pressure is increasing on the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, brought about, in no uncertain terms, by Kosovo, but generally having regard to its failure to cooperate; and, in our submission, this is merely one attempt by the Federal Republic to divert attention, to give it an answer so it can say, "Don't criticise us for our failure to act. Look what we've done: We've had this trial." Your Honours can be rest assured that five minutes after the pressure from the International Community eases on the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, these three accused persons will be released and that any order made will not be genuine. That is the position that the Prosecutor takes. It is the position why we say that the proceedings are merely designed to shield these accused from international criminal responsibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I understand. But a Tribunal is not a political institution, and we cannot not pay attention to that context, but the Judges are doing their work as Judges, and it is true that if we had had the representative today that didn't want to come, the representative of Yugoslavia, he would be entitled -- I would be sure that all questions are answered that have been raised. What is going to authorise you to say that having referred the matter to a Military Court, it is the Military Court itself? It's difficult to use that argument. There are many military people that are subject to military courts. Aside from the coincidence of all kinds of things that have taken place and that we are aware of, that is, you and the International Community, this sudden justice which is coming out in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in Belgrade against these three individuals, legally speaking, what allows you to say that, according to our own texts there are points of reference that it would be justice which is not impartial and which is not independent? Do the penalties not correspond with our own? Have you received information that you could give us, or are you simply remaining with the idea that there is a kind of coincidence which has appeared here and there is a kind of political game going on? But the Judges are not playing a political game but, rather, applying our Rules. Like my colleagues, I am applying them. If it appears that -- to the Prosecutor that any such investigations or criminal proceedings instituted in the courts of the State, the investigation is not impartial or independent and would simply try to shield the accused from international responsibility, you would have to argue to that; that is, shielding the accused from international criminal responsibility or not having diligently prosecuted the case. Therefore, you are asserting, Mr. Prosecutor, that the proceedings which have begun would not be impartial and would not be independent. Is it the form of the court, is it the way the Judges have been chosen, is it the very nature of the charges that have been brought which seem very minor in respect of those that you have brought against those three individuals, or would you prefer to remain with the general coincidence that you have brought out in your request for deferring the cases which have been initiated there?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I can't take it much further other than to say that the history of the matter speaks for itself. It is very clear that this is a State that has consistently failed to cooperate and it is a State that continues to fail to cooperate. There is no question of them being aware of the interest by this Tribunal in these three men, and they have done nothing whatsoever to have them come to The Hague for trial. And, yes, it's political. I make no apologies for that. It is a political issue, but regrettably, at times, politics and law must become intertwined in issues and politics do become entwined in legal issues, and that certainly would be the case here. I might remind Your Honours that I also make this application on the basis of paragraph 3 of Rule 9. I don't rest entirely on paragraph 2, I rest on paragraph 3 as well, which is the fact that it is very closely related to our investigations, of which Your Honours are no doubt aware, we have already had one trial with the accused person Dokmanovic who, unfortunately, died, but Your Honours are aware that these proceedings are very closely connected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, these are the very same legal and factual points. Thank you very much, Mr. Prosecutor. I am now turning to my colleagues. Do you have any questions? Yes, there is possibly one question. I am asking for further clarification that might be helpful. You were mentioning proceedings before the Military Court, Mr. Prosecutor. This was instituted quite recently, wasn't it? Was that in November? You reminded us of it previously. Were you informed of the fact that they were going to initiate proceedings or did the attache or the ambassador or the authorities or else your liaison office in Belgrade mention that they had intentions in that sense? It would be interesting for the Judges to know. Had the Republic of Yugoslavia told you several months ago already that they planned to initiate proceedings, or is this a rather recent announcement? Did this get communicated to you together with the resolution from the Security Council, at that same time?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, it didn't come through the Security Council. It was a letter directed to the Prosecutor, and it is a letter dated the 18th of November, 1998, and it was delivered to our office in Belgrade. It is all set out in detail, Your Honours, in our proposal, in particular --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: -- in the schedule to the proposal. I can go through that if Your Honour wishes me to go through the schedule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: No, that won't be necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: A copy of the letter is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I had another question for you, Mr. Prosecutor. The three people involved, they would be deferred as accused or only as witnesses before this Tribunal Court -- the Military Court, I mean? What was their status there?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That's uncertain, Your Honours. They say from the letter to us that they will be required to come before them and to give testimony, but it doesn't indicate anywhere that they have been charged with anything. It may be that as a result of their testimony, that might happen. I don't know. But it is not suggested in the letter; it is merely suggested that they will come before the Tribunal, the Military Tribunal, and testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Fine. Well, failing other questions, unless Mr. Fourmy has any special questions -- no, that doesn't seem to be the case -- there are no new facts. This being so -- well, Judge Rodrigues, did you have another question? Did you want to mention something else? No? We will give you our decision as soon as possible. Thank you very much for providing us with all this information. But I wanted to give the floor, yes, after all, to Judge Rodrigues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I wanted to inform you of the factors that I, in my capacity as judge on duty, I was seized of two requests or motions from the Prosecutor: There is one motion in which the Prosecutor -- but before going into that, I should say that both motions were under seal, so there may be a problem here. May I go to the merits of these two motions in public or not, because I believe that these motions are very closely connected to the subject matter?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Are you aware of the contents of the two motions which were put before the judge on duty, who was Judge Rodrigues? The two Judges are aware of the matter because we were informed by our colleague. So there is the wish to join the two litigations. Do we want to mention this in public or do we move to closed session?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, if we are to discuss them, I would request that we go into closed session because they are not matters which we would wish to discuss in public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Fine. Fine. We shall do so.
